topics.title: Object Pool Pattern for High-Performance C++
topics.description: Reusing expensive-to-construct objects from a pre-allocated pool to eliminate dynamic heap allocation overhead.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Object Pool Pattern maintains a cache of pre-allocated initialized objects, leasing them to clients and reclaiming them upon completion instead of allocating on the heap.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Frequent new and delete calls fragment heap memory and cause latency spikes in high-performance systems.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Pre-allocate $N$ objects in a vector/queue. acquire() returns an object; custom deleter returns it to the pool upon destruction.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Combine with std::unique_ptr and custom deleters for seamless RAII automatic recycling.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when object creation/destruction cost is high and objects are reused frequently.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use for simple, lightweight structs where standard stack allocation is faster.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Zero heap fragmentation; deterministic high-throughput performance.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires resetting dirty object state before recycling.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Fixed-size Pool, Dynamic Growing Pool, Thread-Safe Pool.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to reset state before reuse, leaking dirty data across requests.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How can std::unique_ptr be used to automate object recycling in an Object Pool?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: By passing a custom lambda deleter to std::unique_ptr that pushes the raw pointer back into the pool's internal collection instead of calling delete.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement a 100-bullet pre-allocated BulletPool.

sections.content: Mastering Object Pool Pattern for High-Performance C++ is essential for advanced C++ systems design.

topics.title: Repository & Data Access Object (DAO) Patterns
topics.description: Decoupling domain business logic from database persistence layers.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Repository Pattern mediates between domain and data mapping layers, providing a collection-like interface (find(), save(), remove()) for domain entities.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Mixing SQL queries directly in domain business logic makes testing impossible and ties business rules to database schemas.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Domain code talks to IUserRepository. Repository handles SQL/NoSQL mapping.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Repository mimics an in-memory collection of domain entities.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Domain-Driven Design enterprise applications, microservice persistence tiers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use in all applications that persist domain entities to external storage.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not create repositories for individual non-aggregate child objects.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Clean abstraction; trivial in-memory mock testing.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Adds abstraction layer over database queries.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Generic Repository, Specific Domain Aggregate Repository.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Leaking database connection/SQL types through repository interface methods.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between Repository and DAO?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: DAO is a low-level database mapping abstraction (table CRUD operations). Repository is a higher-level Domain-Driven Design pattern representing an in-memory collection of complete domain Aggregates.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem

topics.title: Service Locator vs Dependency Injection
topics.description: Comparing Dependency Injection and Service Locator: Why DI is superior for testability and explicit dependencies.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Service Locator is a central registry where classes look up dependencies. Dependency Injection passes dependencies directly via constructor.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Service Locator hides true dependencies inside class method bodies, making dependencies invisible from class signatures.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: DI makes dependencies explicit in the constructor signature. Service Locator uses a global locator singleton.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Prefer Constructor Dependency Injection over Service Locator.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use Dependency Injection as the default standard.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Avoid Service Locator in modern object-oriented architectures.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Explicit contracts and compile-time verification of dependencies.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Constructor parameter lists can grow if not modularized.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Constructor DI, Setter DI, Ambient Context.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Using Service Locator to hide 15 dependencies inside a class.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is Service Locator considered an anti-pattern compared to Dependency Injection?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because Service Locator hides class dependencies, introduces a global singleton dependency, and makes unit testing error-prone due to shared state.
